LBNL Report #2001653 5.2 Mitigating SDF Computational Constraints Since its advent, the SDF technology has involved computational tradeoffs. For example, more reliable SLAM3 can be readily achieved by widening a loop-closure algorithm’s search space. Likewise, smaller sized reconstruction voxels can provide improved fidelity, but also may not - particularly if the information in the collected data is insufficient to support finer voxelization. In the case that smaller voxelization is not beneficial, a monitoring algorithm could be developed and employed in real-time to ensure that voxel sizes were dynamically adjusted to ensure appropriate fidelity, but such an algorithm would require additional computational burdens, or hierarchical reconstruction approaches could be implemented. Also, most uncertainty quantification algorithms are computationally costly and are not typically employed in real-time operation of SDF systems. The computational constraints have been managed through two concurrent SDF technology philosophies: manually configure the real-time SDF algorithms to perform the best one can expect, givenknownsystemconstraintsandtheexpectedsizeoftheproblem; ORensuresufficientcompute resources to successfully collect all the data - rather than allowing sensor driver threads to lag behind and result in dropped data - and use sophisticated algorithms to be run post-hoc and often at slower-than-real-time speeds, even with computers that have significantly greater resources than the computers fielded in the handheld LAMP systems. Suffice to say, implementing many of the newer SDF algorithm developments onboard fielded systems would require improvements in computational efficiency (e.g., through application of mathematically-inspired approaches to simplify or prioritize calculations), development of abilities toanalyzedataoff-board(e.g. throughcloudcomputing),orboth. In such scenarios, it could suffice to run algorithms online that ensure data of sufficient quality and/or quantity is collected. Similarly, if autonomous platforms are carrying the SDF systems, it may also be useful to develop low-fidelity real-time algorithms that can guide acquisition, while still maintaining confidence that offline algorithms will produce ‘final’ data products that meet requirements. The entirety of this section’s discussion is also made with the explicit acknowledgment that computational efficiency continues rapid improvement through hardware advances (e.g., [74] and [76]), yet often those advances require software development. Much of the SDF software stack developed at LBNL has been adapted to be compatible with GPU processors, but use of tensor processing units (TPUs) and directly training AI methods to accelerate sophisticated calculations has not yet occurred.
